b. Spherical Aberration in a Lens

Spherical aberration is an inability of a lens to focus the paraxial rays and marginal rays at the same point on the principal axis. The spherical aberration of the lens is due to its spherical shape. The rays passing through the lens close to its centre (paraxial rays) are focused farther away than rays passing through a circular zone near its rim (marginal rays). Images formed by the lens having large apertures are therefore not sharp but get sharper at smaller apertures. Spherical aberration is found in case of near objects and it is positive for the convex lens and negative for the concave lens.
[Fig.18.9, spherical aberration in a convex lens]
[Fig.18.10, Spherical aberration in a concave lens]

Consider a pointed object (O) has been placed on the principal axis of convex lens L so that paraxial rays from O are focused at point Ip(longer distance) whereas marginal rays are focused at point Im(shorter distance) on the other side of the lens. The image is not sharp at any point on the axis. If the screen is placed perpendicular to the axis, then the image appears as a circular patch of diameter AB as shown in figure 18.9. The spherical aberration in the convex lens is shown in figure 18.10.

To remove spherical aberration in a lens, essentially its focal length for each zone must be made equal so that refracted rays meet at the same point. Practically it is impossible. Therefore, the spherical aberration in a lens can only be reduced but cannot be removed completely.
